# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardium, leading to progressive ventricular wall thickening, diastolic dysfunction, and ultimately restrictive cardiomyopathy and heart failure [1]. Once considered rare and uniformly fatal, CA is now increasingly recognized as an underdiagnosed cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and aortic stenosis, particularly in older adults [2]. Advances in non-invasive imaging and the advent of disease-modifying therapies have transformed the diagnostic and therapeutic landscape [3].

## Types and Pathophysiology

The two predominant forms affecting the heart are immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloidosis and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis [4]. AL amyloidosis arises from a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia producing misfolded light chains and carries a particularly poor prognosis when cardiac involvement is present [5]. ATTR amyloidosis results from destabilization of the transthyretin tetramer, which dissociates and aggregates into fibrils; it occurs in wild-type (ATTRwt, formerly senile systemic amyloidosis) and hereditary (ATTRv) forms [6]. The Val122Ile variant is notably prevalent among individuals of African ancestry, while Val30Met is common in endemic regions such as Portugal and Japan [7]. The mechanisms of cardiac toxicity involve both mechanical disruption of myocardial architecture and direct proteotoxicity, especially from circulating light chains in AL disease [8].

## Clinical Presentation

Patients typically present with signs of progressive heart failure, often with preserved ejection fraction, fatigue, and exertional dyspnea [9]. Extracardiac features may provide diagnostic clues: carpal tunnel syndrome (frequently bilateral and preceding cardiac symptoms by years), lumbar spinal stenosis, and biceps tendon rupture are characteristic of ATTR amyloidosis [10]. AL amyloidosis may additionally manifest with periorbital purpura, macroglossia, nephrotic-range proteinuria, and autonomic neuropathy [11]. Arrhythmias, including atrial fibrillation and conduction disease, are common, and low QRS voltage relative to wall thickness on electrocardiography is a classic but inconsistent finding [12].

## Diagnosis

Echocardiography typically demonstrates increased left ventricular wall thickness with a characteristic "apical sparing" pattern of longitudinal strain [13]. Cardiac magnetic resonance reveals diffuse late gadolinium enhancement and elevated extracellular volume, reflecting the expanded interstitium [14]. A landmark advance was the recognition that bone-avid radiotracer scintigraphy (technetium-99m pyrophosphate or DPD) can non-invasively diagnose ATTR-CA with high specificity when accompanied by exclusion of a monoclonal protein [15]. The non-biopsy diagnostic algorithm—combining grade 2–3 cardiac uptake on scintigraphy with negative serum and urine immunofixation and serum free light-chain assays—obviates endomyocardial biopsy in many patients [16]. However, any positive monoclonal screen mandates further evaluation, as scintigraphy can be falsely positive in AL amyloidosis [17]. Cardiac biomarkers, particularly N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide and troponin, are central to staging systems for both AL and ATTR disease [18].

## Treatment

Management has evolved dramatically. For AL amyloidosis, therapy targets the underlying plasma cell clone; the addition of daratumumab to bortezomib-based regimens has improved hematologic and organ responses [19]. Autologous stem cell transplantation remains an option for carefully selected patients [20]. For ATTR-CA, tafamidis, a transthyretin stabilizer, reduced all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations in the ATTR-ACT trial and is now a cornerstone of therapy [21]. Gene-silencing approaches, including the small interfering RNA agents patisiran and the more recent vutrisiran, have shown benefit in ATTR amyloidosis with polyneuropathy and cardiomyopathy [22, 23]. Acoramidis, another stabilizer, demonstrated favorable outcomes in the ATTRibute-CM trial [24]. Emerging strategies include CRISPR-based in vivo gene editing of TTR, which produced durable reductions in serum transthyretin [25], and antibody-mediated amyloid depletion therapies under investigation [26].

Supportive management of heart failure in CA differs from conventional approaches: loop diuretics are the mainstay, while many patients tolerate beta-blockers and renin-angiotensin inhibitors poorly [27]. Anticoagulation is generally recommended in atrial fibrillation given elevated thromboembolic risk, even in sinus rhythm in some cases [28]. Transcatheter aortic valve replacement may benefit patients with concomitant aortic stenosis and ATTR-CA [29].

## Prognosis and Conclusion

Prognosis depends on amyloid type, cardiac stage, and timeliness of diagnosis; untreated AL-CA historically carried a median survival of months, while earlier detection and modern therapy substantially improve outcomes [30]. Heightened clinical awareness, validated imaging algorithms, and effective disease-modifying agents have shifted CA from an untreatable diagnosis to a manageable condition. Continued progress in early detection and novel therapeutics promises further improvements in survival and quality of life.
